title: Interactions within Ecosystems
seo_title: Secondary 2 Science: Ecosystems Worksheets (Lower Secondary Science with Answers)
standard_text: Describe an ecosystem as a community interacting with its physical environment; explain how physical factors such as air, water, temperature, light, minerals and pH affect survival; describe predator-prey, mutualism and parasitism; describe the flow of energy through food chains and food webs, including photosynthesis and respiration, and nutrient recycling by decomposers; evaluate the impact of human activities on the environment (summary of the MOE Lower Secondary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 2 science worksheets for Singapore students on ecosystems: physical factors, predator-prey, mutualism and parasitism, food webs, energy flow and decomposers. With answers.
key_big: Organisms interact with each other and with their environment.
body_html:
How to think about it

An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and with the physical environment.

  • Physical factors: air, water, temperature, light, minerals and pH.
  • Relationships: predator-prey, mutualism (both benefit), parasitism (parasite benefits, host harmed), competition.
  • Energy enters by photosynthesis and flows along food chains; only about 10% passes to the next level. Energy is lost as heat in respiration.
  • Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead matter back to the soil.
Example

Bees pollinate flowers and get nectar. Relationship?

Both benefit

Answer: mutualism

Example

Producers trap 10 000 kJ. About how much reaches the primary consumers?

About 10% passes on

Answer: 1000 kJ

Common mistakes

  • Saying mutualism harms one organism. In mutualism both benefit.
  • Saying energy is recycled. Nutrients are recycled; energy flows and is lost as heat.
  • Leaving out the physical environment: an ecosystem includes non-living factors.
  • Thinking removing one organism affects only its predator.

faq.q: What is the difference between mutualism and parasitism?
faq.a: In mutualism both organisms benefit. In parasitism the parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

faq.q: Why is energy lost along a food chain?
faq.a: Each organism uses energy for respiration and life processes, and much of it is lost as heat. Only about 10% passes on.

c: Energy is lost as heat at each step, but nutrients are returned to the soil by decomposers and used again.

items.e: The Sun keeps supplying new energy.

c: It is stored in the Sun.

It is recycled back to the producers.
items.e: Energy flows through a food chain and is not recycled.

items.q: Why are food webs more stable when they have more species?

items.q: Why do predator and prey populations rise and fall in cycles?

More prey means more food for predators; then more predators eat more prey, so prey fall, then predators fall.
items.e: Predator–prey cycles.

items.q: Why is it important to conserve the mangroves at Sungei Buloh?

items.e: Removing them affects the whole ecosystem.

items.q: A farmer sprays a pesticide that kills all the insects in a field. Which is a likely result?
c: Birds that eat insects lose their food, and plants that need pollinators make fewer seeds.
items.e: Organisms in an ecosystem are interdependent.

items.q: Corals turn white (bleach) when sea temperatures rise. What does this show?

Corals are plants that need more light.
items.e: Coral bleaching is linked to global warming.

items.q: Rats were reduced on an island. Then the number of birds that nest on the ground rose. Why?
c: Fewer rats ate the birds' eggs and chicks.
items.e: Removing a predator affects its prey.

items.q: Why is energy not recycled in a food chain like minerals are?
c: Plants make new energy from soil.
Energy is lost as heat to the surroundings at each level.
It is stored in the predator forever.
items.e: Energy flows, matter cycles.
